newsitem.title: KENYA: Reform leaders call rallies across Kenya on Monday.
newsitem.headline: Reform leaders call rallies across Kenya on Monday.

text.p: An opposition-backed reform alliance called on Thursday for rallies across Kenya on Monday and police clashed with stone-throwing students in the capital Nairobi.
Some 1,000 students marched in Nairobi, protesting against a proposed bill that students who fail to pay fees should be expelled. They were addressed by opposition politicians at parliament.
Students threw stones at cars near Nairobi University and clashed with riot police who fired teargas canisters and used batons to disperse them. A policeman was hurt by a stone, witnesses said.

The National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) called its rallies for July 7, in Kiswahili known as "Saba Saba" which commemorates a Nairobi rally seven years ago when at least 20 people were killed.
"The NCEC calls upon all Kenyans to commemorate this day by turning up for planned provincial rallies," said NCEC member John Munuve before naming some 50 locations across the country.
The National Convention groups opposition parties, churches, human rights and other bodies. Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi's government has outlawed the rallies and vowed to stop them taking place.
"We shall maintain peace if we are not provoked by the police," said opposition parliamentarian James Orengo, arguing the rallies were not illegal but were "educational meetings".
Munuve said major meetings would be held in the towns of Kisumu and Eldoret in western Kenya, Nakuru, northwest of Nairobi, and in Wajir in the northeast corner of the country.

Opposition activists who declined to be named said they expected trouble. They said the list of some 50 rally locations was long to put pressure on security forces, stretching them across the country.

The NCEC said that in some places prayers would be held and there was no uniform type of political action to press the Moi government for constitutional reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections due later this year. No date for the polls has been set.

Richard Leakey, secretary-general of the Safina opposition party which has not been registered by authorities, said in a statement backing the rallies: "The issue is not whether Mr Moi must go (as president), the demand is for reform."
Leakey, who is also Kenya's former wildlife guardian and a world renowned palaeontologist, said:

"Everyone, everywhere in Kenya should join the Monday action. Stay away from work, close businesses for the day, freeze the country to show Mr Moi and his dwindling supporters the time for dialogue and change has come.
"Safina urges that there be no violence and we hope the security forces and the supporters for reform will not allow themselves to be provoked by thugs and evil people," he added.
The Electoral Commission said on Wednesday it believed more than nine million people had registered to vote this year, compared with 7.8 million for Kenya's first multi-party polls in 1992.
Moi said on Wednesday the opposition planned chaos on Monday and was inciting youths to take part in riots in Nairobi. The president argues there is no time for reforms before polls.
Despite the opposition campaign, Moi, 73, looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for five more years because of electoral rules and deep personal and ethnic splits within the opposition.

The opposition disrupted reading of the budget in parliament on June 19 before a punch-up between politicians. But only a few hundred students challenged a heavy police and paramilitary presence the same day on the semi-deserted streets of Nairobi.
One person died and scores of shops were looted in two days of rioting in Nairobi after security forces broke up a reform rally on May 31 which the government had declared illegal.
